BPC-157.summary: Synthetic peptide promoted for tendon, gut and wound healing; supporting data come almost entirely from animal studies.
BPC-157.note: The FDA has flagged evidence gaps and safety concerns for it.
BPC-157.overview:
BPC-157 ("body protection compound 157") is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide modeled on a fragment of a protein found in human gastric juice. It has no approved medical use anywhere and is sold mainly as a "research chemical" and through compounding channels.

In appearance and recovery circles it is promoted for tendon, ligament, gut and wound healing, on the argument that faster repair supports training and aesthetics. The supporting literature comes overwhelmingly from rodent experiments, largely from a single research group, and a 2025 systematic review found almost no human clinical data.
BPC-157.mechanism: Preclinical work suggests BPC-157 may influence angiogenesis (including VEGF signaling), growth-hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts, nitric oxide pathways and the FAK-paxillin axis, which together could speed cell migration and tissue repair. These mechanisms are proposed from cell and animal studies and have not been confirmed in controlled human trials.
BPC-157.risks: Human safety data are minimal, so the risk profile is largely unknown. Concerns include unregulated product purity and identity, injection-site problems, and a theoretical concern that pro-angiogenic activity could be undesirable in people with cancer risk. It is not FDA-approved, US regulators have flagged evidence and safety gaps for compounding, and it is prohibited by WADA for tested athletes.

TB-500.summary: Vendor name for synthetic thymosin beta-4 or a fragment of it, promoted for tissue repair; preclinical evidence, and product identity varies.
TB-500.overview:
TB-500 is the name used by research-peptide vendors for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) or a fragment of it; the exact molecule sold varies by supplier. Tβ4 itself is a 43-amino-acid protein that is abundant in most human cells and binds actin.

In recovery and looksmaxxing communities it is marketed for tendon, muscle and skin repair, often stacked with BPC-157. The established research on full-length Tβ4 involves wound, eye and cardiac repair; evidence that vendor TB-500 products do the same in healthy people is essentially absent.
TB-500.mechanism: Tβ4 sequesters monomeric actin, which influences cell migration, and in animal models it has been linked to angiogenesis, reduced inflammation and improved cell survival in injured tissue. Whether the shorter fragment sold as TB-500 reproduces these effects has not been well established.
TB-500.risks: Human safety data for the vendor products are lacking, and product identity and purity are inconsistent. Pro-angiogenic activity raises a theoretical concern in people with cancer risk. TB-500 is not an approved drug and is banned by WADA, and a high-profile Australian sports supplement scandal involved thymosin beta-4.

KPV.summary: Alpha-MSH-derived anti-inflammatory tripeptide; evidence is from cell and mouse studies, with no completed human trials.
KPV.overview:
KPV is a tripeptide (lysine-proline-valine) corresponding to the C-terminal end of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH). It retains anti-inflammatory activity without the pigmentation effects of the full hormone.

It is sold as a research chemical and discussed in peptide communities for gut inflammation, skin irritation and general "inflammation control." Almost all evidence is from cell and mouse models, particularly colitis, and no completed human trials support cosmetic or recovery claims.
KPV.mechanism: In preclinical studies KPV enters inflamed intestinal cells through the PepT1 transporter and dampens NF-κB and MAPK signaling, lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines. Its action appears to be partly independent of classical melanocortin receptors.
KPV.risks: Human safety and efficacy data are lacking. Vendor products are unregulated with variable purity and stability. It is not approved as a drug, and self-injecting or ingesting unregulated peptides carries contamination and unknown-effect risks.

Thymosin alpha-1.summary: Immune-modulating peptide with human research in medical conditions such as hepatitis B and infections; no cosmetic evidence.
Thymosin alpha-1.overview:
Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide first isolated from thymus tissue. Its synthetic form, thymalfasin, is approved as an immune modulator in a number of countries (not by the US FDA) for conditions such as chronic hepatitis B and as an adjunct in other settings.

It appears in longevity and biohacking discussions as an "immune optimizer," but its human research concerns medical conditions such as infections, sepsis and cancer adjunct care, not appearance. No good evidence of cosmetic benefit has been published.
Thymosin alpha-1.mechanism: Thymosin alpha-1 is thought to act on Toll-like receptors on dendritic cells and other immune cells, promoting T-cell maturation and cytokine signaling that enhances adaptive immune responses.
Thymosin alpha-1.risks: In clinical studies it is generally well tolerated, with mild injection-site reactions most common, but trial quality is heterogeneous and safety reporting inconsistent. Immune stimulation is a concern in autoimmune disease or transplant settings. Gray-market products are unregulated, and evidence supporting use in healthy people is lacking.

Curcumin.summary: Turmeric polyphenol with anti-inflammatory activity; reviews report modest arthritis benefits, and plain curcumin is poorly absorbed.
Curcumin.overview:
Curcumin is the main yellow polyphenol of turmeric (Curcuma longa). It is widely sold as a supplement and used in cooking and traditional medicine.

In recovery and appearance contexts it is taken for joint soreness, general inflammation and skin health. Systematic reviews report modest benefits for arthritis symptoms and inflammatory markers, though trial quality is mixed and plain curcumin is poorly absorbed.
Curcumin.mechanism: Curcumin modulates inflammatory signaling such as NF-κB and COX-2 and has antioxidant activity in laboratory studies. Oral bioavailability is very low because of poor solubility and rapid metabolism, which is why piperine, lipid formulations and other delivery technologies are used.
Curcumin.risks: Generally well tolerated, with occasional gastrointestinal upset. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported with high-bioavailability products, and it may interact with anticoagulants. Supplement quality varies, and adulteration with lead-containing pigments has been documented. Legal as a dietary supplement.

N-Acetylcysteine.summary: Glutathione precursor and established medicine for acetaminophen overdose and mucus thinning, also sold as a supplement.
N-Acetylcysteine.overview:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is an established medicine used as the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose and as a mucus-thinning agent, and is also sold as a supplement.

In recovery and appearance communities it is used as a glutathione precursor and antioxidant. Beyond its approved uses, evidence for skin, hair or recovery benefits is limited, though it has been studied for psychiatric and compulsive-behavior conditions.
N-Acetylcysteine.mechanism: NAC supplies cysteine, the rate-limiting building block for glutathione synthesis, and can also act as a direct reducing agent and modulate glutamate signaling.
N-Acetylcysteine.risks: Common side effects are nausea and other gastrointestinal upset; a sulfur odor is commonly noted. Intravenous use carries anaphylactoid reaction risk. Its US regulatory status as a supplement has been disputed because it is also an approved drug, though it remains widely available.

Glycine.summary: Main amino acid in collagen, sold as a low-cost supplement; small trials report improved subjective sleep.
Glycine.overview:
Glycine is the smallest proteinogenic amino acid and makes up roughly a third of the amino acid residues in collagen. It is inexpensive, sold as a powder supplement, and consumed in the diet through gelatin and protein foods.

In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is used to support collagen turnover and sleep quality. Small trials suggest improved subjective sleep, while direct evidence that supplementation visibly changes skin or connective tissue is limited.
Glycine.mechanism: Glycine acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem and, via NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, lowers core body temperature, which is the proposed route to better sleep. It is also a substrate for collagen, creatine and glutathione synthesis.
Glycine.risks: Very well tolerated at typical intakes; mild gastrointestinal upset or drowsiness can occur. It is a food-grade supplement with no particular legal restrictions. Interactions with some antipsychotics (e.g. clozapine) have been noted.

Taurine.summary: Sulfur-containing amino acid common in energy drinks; reviews report small metabolic and performance effects and thin appearance evidence.
Taurine.overview:
Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino sulfonic acid found in high concentrations in muscle, heart, retina and brain. It is common in energy drinks and available as a standalone supplement.

In recovery and longevity discussions it is promoted for exercise performance, cell protection and general health. Reviews show small effects on some metabolic and performance outcomes, and evidence for appearance-related benefits is limited.
Taurine.mechanism: Taurine contributes to osmoregulation, bile-salt conjugation, calcium handling and antioxidant defense, and may modulate inhibitory GABA and glycine receptors. How oral supplementation translates to measurable benefits in healthy adults has not been well established.
Taurine.risks: Considered safe at typical intakes, with rare mild gastrointestinal effects. Most health concerns about energy drinks relate to caffeine rather than taurine. It is legal and sold as a supplement and food additive.

Boswellia serrata.summary: Resin-derived botanical studied for inflammation and joint symptoms, with modest osteoarthritis findings in small trials.
Boswellia serrata.overview:
Boswellia serrata is a tree native to India whose resin (Indian frankincense) contains boswellic acids. Extracts are sold as joint and anti-inflammatory supplements, often alongside curcumin.

Its main evidence base is osteoarthritis symptoms, where meta-analyses report modest improvements in pain and function, though trials are small and often industry-linked. Relevance to appearance is indirect, via training recovery and joint comfort.
Boswellia serrata.mechanism: Boswellic acids, especially acetyl-keto-beta-boswellic acid, inhibit 5-lipoxygenase and reduce leukotriene production, and may suppress some inflammatory cytokines.
Boswellia serrata.risks: Adverse effects are generally mild, such as stomach upset or diarrhea. Product standardization varies, and safety in pregnancy has not been established. Legal as a dietary supplement; over-harvesting of wild trees is an ecological concern.

Bromelain.summary: Pineapple-derived enzyme mixture studied for swelling and inflammation, with mixed and often small study results.
Bromelain.overview:
Bromelain is a mixture of protein-digesting enzymes extracted mainly from pineapple stem. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing; a topical form is approved for debriding burn wounds.

In appearance contexts it is used to reduce post-procedure swelling and bruising (for example after cosmetic surgery) and general inflammation. Study results are mixed and often small.
Bromelain.mechanism: Bromelain's proteolytic activity is thought to modulate inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins and to affect fibrin breakdown. How much active enzyme survives digestion and reaches tissue after oral dosing is uncertain.
Bromelain.risks: Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to pineapple. It may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and interact with some antibiotics. Supplement potency is inconsistent. Legal as a supplement.

NMN.summary: NAD+ precursor that raises blood NAD+ in human trials; visible rejuvenation or lifespan benefit has not been demonstrated.
NMN.overview:
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a nucleotide that the body converts into NAD+, a coenzyme central to energy metabolism. It is sold as an oral supplement, and its regulatory status as a supplement has been contested in the United States.

It is promoted for anti-aging, energy and skin appearance. Human trials show it raises blood NAD+ levels, but clear evidence of visible rejuvenation or lifespan benefit is lacking.
NMN.mechanism: NMN is converted to NAD+ via the NAD salvage pathway; NAD+ is a cofactor for sirtuins and PARPs and for redox reactions. NAD+ levels decline with age in some tissues, which is the stated rationale for supplementation.
NMN.risks: Short-term human trials report good tolerability, with mild gastrointestinal or flushing effects possible. Long-term safety has not been established, and theoretical concerns about NAD+ boosting in existing cancers remain unresolved. Product quality varies.

Nicotinamide riboside.summary: Vitamin B3 form and NAD+ precursor; trials show raised blood NAD+, with modest or inconsistent functional benefits.
Nicotinamide riboside.overview:
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 and a precursor to NAD+. It is sold as an oral supplement and has been tested in a number of human trials.

It is marketed for healthy aging and energy. Trials consistently show increased blood NAD+ levels, while reported benefits for muscle, metabolism or appearance have been modest or inconsistent.
Nicotinamide riboside.mechanism: NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases to NMN and then converted to NAD+, supporting sirtuin and DNA-repair enzyme activity.
Nicotinamide riboside.risks: Well tolerated in studies, with mild nausea, flushing or digestive effects at higher intakes. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US and novel food approval in the EU; product quality varies.

Resveratrol.summary: Polyphenol from grape skins studied for sirtuin signaling; human evidence for longevity or visible anti-aging is insufficient.
Resveratrol.overview:
Resveratrol is a polyphenol found in grape skins, berries and peanuts, popularized by the "French paradox" and by early sirtuin-activation research. It is sold as a supplement and used in some skincare products.

It is promoted for longevity and skin health. Human trials show small effects on some metabolic markers, but evidence for longevity or visible anti-aging is insufficient, and its poor bioavailability limits interpretation.
Resveratrol.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms include activation of SIRT1 and AMPK and antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Some of the sirtuin findings have been disputed, and oral resveratrol is rapidly metabolized, leaving little free compound in circulation.
Resveratrol.risks: Usually well tolerated; high doses can cause gastrointestinal upset. It may interact with anticoagulants and drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes. Legal as a supplement; product quality varies.

Spermidine.summary: Naturally occurring polyamine linked to autophagy; observational data link intake to lower mortality, while randomized human data are preliminary.
Spermidine.overview:
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine present in all cells and in foods such as wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese. It is sold as a supplement, often as wheat germ extract.

It is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity compound. Observational data link higher dietary intake to lower mortality, but randomized human evidence is preliminary and no cosmetic benefit has been established.
Spermidine.mechanism: Spermidine induces autophagy in model organisms, partly through inhibition of the acetyltransferase EP300, and is required for hypusination of eIF5A, which supports mitochondrial function and immune cell activity.
Spermidine.risks: Generally well tolerated at studied intakes; mild gastrointestinal effects are possible. Polyamines are also needed by rapidly growing cells, so theoretical concerns exist in cancer settings. Legal as a supplement or novel food in many regions.

Urolithin A.summary: Gut-bacteria metabolite of pomegranate and walnut compounds; early trials report improved muscle endurance in older adults.
Urolithin A.overview:
Urolithin A is a metabolite produced by gut bacteria from ellagitannins in pomegranate, walnuts and berries. Only some people produce it efficiently, which is the rationale given for direct supplementation.

It is marketed for muscle and mitochondrial health in aging. Early randomized trials report improvements in some muscle endurance measures in older adults, while effects on strength and appearance are small or not shown.
Urolithin A.mechanism: Urolithin A is proposed to induce mitophagy, the clearance of damaged mitochondria, via PINK1/Parkin-related pathways, and to influence AMPK and other stress-response signaling.
Urolithin A.risks: Short-term trials report good tolerability. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US, and regulatory status elsewhere varies. Most trials were sponsored by the commercial supplier.

Coenzyme Q10.summary: Mitochondrial electron-transport cofactor made by the body; cosmetic evidence is limited and mostly from small or topical studies.
Coenzyme Q10.overview:
Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble molecule that carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and acts as an antioxidant. The body makes it, and levels fall with age and with statin use.

It is sold as an oral supplement and is added to some anti-aging creams. Evidence for cosmetic effects is limited and mostly from small or topical studies, while its best-supported uses concern cardiovascular and mitochondrial contexts.
Coenzyme Q10.mechanism: CoQ10 shuttles electrons in oxidative phosphorylation and regenerates other antioxidants such as vitamin E. Topically it has been studied for reducing oxidative damage in skin.
Coenzyme Q10.risks: Generally well tolerated, with occasional digestive upset or insomnia. It may reduce the effect of warfarin. Legal as a supplement; absorption varies with formulation.

Alpha-lipoic acid.summary: Redox-active antioxidant and mitochondrial cofactor, with established use in diabetic neuropathy and limited appearance evidence.
Alpha-lipoic acid.overview:
Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) is a sulfur-containing cofactor for mitochondrial enzymes and a redox-active antioxidant, available as a supplement and in some skincare products.

Its best-established human use is symptom relief in diabetic neuropathy. Claims for skin and anti-aging benefits rest on limited evidence.
Alpha-lipoic acid.mechanism: ALA and its reduced form dihydrolipoic acid scavenge reactive oxygen species and regenerate other antioxidants, and may influence insulin signaling and NF-κB activity.
Alpha-lipoic acid.risks: Generally well tolerated; nausea, rash and, rarely, hypoglycemia in people on glucose-lowering drugs can occur. Legal as a supplement.

Fisetin.summary: Flavonol studied as a senolytic candidate; mouse studies report health and lifespan effects, and human data are limited to early trials.
Fisetin.overview:
Fisetin is a flavonol found in strawberries, apples and onions, sold as a supplement and discussed as a candidate senolytic, a compound that selectively clears senescent cells.

It gained attention after mouse studies reported extended health and lifespan. Human data are limited to early or ongoing trials, and no appearance benefit has been demonstrated.
Fisetin.mechanism: In cell and mouse studies fisetin reduced senescent-cell burden and inflammatory signaling, possibly via pathways involving PI3K/AKT and mTOR modulation, along with antioxidant effects.
Fisetin.risks: Human safety data at the doses discussed online are sparse. Possible interactions with drugs are not well characterized. Legal as a supplement, but not an approved therapy for any condition.

Quercetin.summary: Antioxidant flavonoid with limited, mixed human evidence; paired with dasatinib in senolytic research.
Quercetin.overview:
Quercetin is a plant flavonol abundant in onions, capers and apples, sold as a supplement. It is also the 'Q' in the dasatinib plus quercetin senolytic combination studied in aging research.

Human evidence for benefits is limited and mixed, covering blood pressure, allergy and inflammation. Cosmetic benefits have not been established.
Quercetin.mechanism: Quercetin has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and stabilizes mast cells in laboratory studies. In senolytic research it is paired with dasatinib to clear senescent cells in preliminary human work. Oral bioavailability is low.
Quercetin.risks: Usually well tolerated at supplemental doses; high doses may cause headache or stomach upset and could affect kidney function or drug metabolism. Legal as a supplement.

Rapamycin.summary: Prescription mTOR inhibitor that extends lifespan in mice; human anti-aging benefit has not been demonstrated.
Rapamycin.overview:
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrolide originally found in a soil bacterium from Easter Island. It is a prescription immunosuppressant used in transplantation and certain rare diseases.

It is the best-replicated lifespan-extending drug in mice, which has driven off-label interest in humans. Human anti-aging benefit is unproven, and a systematic review of human data found limited evidence.
Rapamycin.mechanism: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 (and with chronic use, to some extent mTORC2), a nutrient-sensing growth pathway, which promotes autophagy and reduces protein synthesis and cell growth signaling.
Rapamycin.risks: Prescription-only. Known adverse effects include mouth ulcers, impaired wound healing, elevated lipids, glucose intolerance and increased infection risk, particularly at transplant doses. Off-label use for longevity is unapproved; physician supervision is advised in medical guidance.

Metformin.summary: First-line type 2 diabetes drug with AMPK-related effects; whether it slows aging in healthy people is unproven.
Metformin.overview:
Metformin is a first-line oral drug for type 2 diabetes, with decades of safety data. It is available by prescription.

It is discussed in longevity circles because of observational links to lower mortality and cancer rates in diabetics. Whether it slows aging in healthy people is unproven, and recent reviews express skepticism.
Metformin.mechanism: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity, partly through AMPK activation and mitochondrial complex I inhibition, with downstream effects on mTOR signaling.
Metformin.risks: Common side effects are gastrointestinal upset and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use; rare lactic acidosis occurs mainly with kidney impairment. Some evidence suggests it may blunt exercise adaptations. Prescription-only; off-label use for aging is not approved.

Epitalon.summary: Synthetic tetrapeptide promoted for telomere lengthening; data come mainly from its originating group, with no large independent human trials.
Epitalon.overview:
Epitalon (epithalon) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) developed from an extract of bovine pineal gland by a Russian research group. It is sold as a research chemical.

It is popular in anti-aging communities because of claims that it lengthens telomeres. Most data come from the originating group, animal studies and cell lines, with no large independent human trials.
Epitalon.mechanism: Cell studies report that epitalon can upregulate telomerase or alternative lengthening of telomeres, and it has been proposed to affect melatonin production and gene expression. Whether these mechanisms translate into human anti-aging effects has not been validated.
Epitalon.risks: Human safety data are small and mostly from one research group. It is not approved as a drug by major regulators, product quality is unregulated, and telomerase activation raises theoretical cancer concerns.

MOTS-c.summary: Mitochondria-derived peptide that improved metabolic health in mouse studies; human evidence is limited.
MOTS-c.overview:
MOTS-c is a short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA, first described in 2015. It is sold as a research chemical.

In mouse studies it improved insulin sensitivity and metabolic health, and it is promoted for fat loss, endurance and longevity. Human evidence is limited mainly to observational data and early-phase work on analogs.
MOTS-c.mechanism: MOTS-c is reported to act on the folate-methionine cycle and activate AMPK, shifting cellular metabolism, and may move to the nucleus under stress to regulate gene expression.
MOTS-c.risks: Human safety data are essentially absent for vendor products. It is not an approved drug and is prohibited by anti-doping agencies; purity and identity of gray-market peptides are unreliable.

SS-31.summary: Mitochondria-targeted peptide (elamipretide) developed for rare mitochondrial disease; no cosmetic anti-aging benefit has been demonstrated.
SS-31.overview:
SS-31 (elamipretide) is a synthetic tetrapeptide that targets mitochondria. It has been developed as a drug for rare mitochondrial disease, and gray-market versions circulate as research chemicals.

In longevity discussions it is promoted for energy and anti-aging. Evidence is from disease trials and animal aging studies; no cosmetic anti-aging benefit in healthy people has been demonstrated.
SS-31.mechanism: SS-31 binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is thought to stabilize respiratory complexes, improve electron transport efficiency and reduce reactive oxygen species production.
SS-31.risks: Reported adverse events in trials are mostly injection-site reactions. Long-term safety has not been fully established, and vendor products are unregulated. Any regulatory approval concerns specific rare diseases, not general use.

GlyNAC.summary: Glycine plus NAC combination; small trials from one academic group report improved glutathione and aging-related markers.
GlyNAC.overview:
GlyNAC is a combination of glycine and N-acetylcysteine proposed to restore glutathione levels that decline with age. It is sold as an over-the-counter supplement.

Small trials by one academic group in older adults reported improved glutathione, inflammation markers and some physical function measures. Sample sizes are small, and appearance effects have not been shown.
GlyNAC.mechanism: Cysteine (from NAC) and glycine are the two limiting amino acids for glutathione synthesis, so supplementing both is hypothesized to improve antioxidant capacity and mitochondrial function.
GlyNAC.risks: Adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal, from NAC. Trial doses are large and long-term safety has not been established. Legal as a supplement.

Alpha-ketoglutarate.summary: Citric acid cycle intermediate studied in aging biology; mouse studies report longer lifespan, and human evidence is preliminary.
Alpha-ketoglutarate.overview:
Alpha-ketoglutarate (AKG) is a key intermediate in the citric acid cycle and in amino acid metabolism. It is sold as a supplement, often as calcium AKG.

It attracted longevity interest after mouse studies showed extended lifespan and compressed morbidity. Human evidence is preliminary, with small, company-linked studies and no demonstrated cosmetic benefit.
Alpha-ketoglutarate.mechanism: AKG is a cofactor for dioxygenases involved in epigenetic regulation (such as TET enzymes and histone demethylases) and for collagen hydroxylation, and it links energy and nitrogen metabolism.
Alpha-ketoglutarate.risks: Generally regarded as well tolerated in short-term use, but long-term human safety data are limited. Legal as a supplement. Claims about reduced biological age come from small, non-definitive studies.
